c.tagline: The ancient Inca capital, gateway to Machu Picchu and the Sacred Valley.

taxi.fareNote: Cusco taxis are unmetered; agree the fare before getting in (short in-town rides run about S/5-10). Uber and InDrive have limited coverage, so most rides are hailed on the street or booked by phone.

emergency.note: 105 reaches the national police; 116/106 is for medical/ambulance (SAMU). Altitude sickness (soroche) is the most common traveler issue at 3,400 m - ascend slowly and hydrate.

avoid.reason: Petty theft around San Pedro market and nightlife; avoid walking alone at night in outer areas

hood_desc: The walkable heart of the city around the Plaza de Armas, ringed by the cathedral, colonial arcades, restaurants, and travel agencies; best for first-timers who want every major sight on their doorstep.

Cusco's bohemian artisan quarter of steep cobbled lanes, galleries, cafes, and viewpoints just uphill from the plaza; suits travelers after character, craft shops, and rooftop views (be ready for the climb at altitude).
A lively, local, budget-friendly area around the Eiffel-designed San Pedro Market, five minutes west of the plaza; good for food stalls, cheap eats, and easy transport connections.
One of Cusco's oldest and quietest neighborhoods, climbing west of the center to the 16th-century Santa Ana church and sweeping city views; full of affordable guesthouses and a residential feel.
A modern residential district with wider streets, shopping centers, local markets, and the closest access to the airport and bus terminals; a calmer, more authentic base away from the tourist core.

water.note: Drink bottled, boiled or filtered water; tap water is not safe for visitors.

transit.pay: Pay the flat fare in cash to the driver or fare collector on board - about S/1 (~$0.30) for a city combi ride. There is no rechargeable transit card; carry small coins.
transit.hours: Combis and colectivos run roughly 5am to 10-11pm; after that, taxis (agree the fare first) fill the late-night gap.
transit.note: Cusco has no metro or tram; the compact historic center is best explored on foot, with combis and taxis covering longer trips and the outer districts.

train: PeruRail / Inca Rail to Ollantaytambo & Aguas Calientes (Machu Picchu)
bus: Combis & colectivos to the Sacred Valley

transit.m: Combi or colectivo from outside the terminal to the center, ~20-30 min
Taxi to Plaza de Armas, 15-25 min

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or leaving ~10% at sit-down restaurants for good service is appreciated.

food.name: Cuy al horno
food.desc: Whole oven-roasted guinea pig, the Andean festive dish, served with potatoes, stuffed herbs and huacatay sauce. Order an hour ahead.

places.name: Quinta Eulalia
places.note: Traditional picanteria open more than 60 years; roast cuy in a sunny courtyard.

places.name: La Cusquenita
places.note: Boisterous local picanteria with live Andean music and full traditional plates.

places.name: La Chomba
places.note: Long-standing neighborhood chicheria known for baked cuy and hearty portions.

food.name: Chicharron cusqueno
food.desc: Pork belly simmered then fried in its own fat, piled with mote corn, fried potato, mint and salsa criolla. A weekend breakfast institution.

places.name: Chicharronerias of Pampa del Castillo
places.note: A short street lined with competing chicharron kitchens; pick the busiest one.

places.name: Saylla chicharron row
places.note: Village 20 minutes out that Cusquenos drive to specifically for chicharron.

places.name: La Cusquenita
places.note: Serves the full pork-and-mote plate in town if you do not want to leave the city.

food.name: Chiri uchu
food.desc: Cusco's Corpus Christi dish, eaten cold: guinea pig, chicken, cured pork, seaweed, roe-stuffed sausage, cheese, corn and a maize tortilla.

places.name: Mercado de San Pedro
places.note: Market comedor stalls assemble the platter, most reliably around the Corpus Christi season.

places.name: Plaza San Francisco stalls
places.note: The traditional Corpus Christi chiri uchu fair each June; the definitive place to try it.

places.name: Pachapapa
places.note: Courtyard restaurant that puts Andean classics, including seasonal chiri uchu, on the menu.

food.name: Choclo con queso
food.desc: Giant-kernelled Andean corn boiled and served with a slab of fresh salty cheese; the classic cheap Cusco snack, often eaten standing up.

places.name: Mercado de San Pedro
places.note: Vendors sell it hot by the ear all morning, alongside juices and tamales.

places.name: Mercado de Wanchaq
places.note: Less touristy market where locals shop; good choclo, cheese and fruit stalls.

places.name: Pachapapa
places.note: Sit-down version with anticuchos and a clay-oven kitchen if you want a table.

food.name: Adobo cusqueno
food.desc: Pork shoulder marinated overnight in chicha de jora, garlic and aji panca, then stewed and eaten for Sunday breakfast with crusty bread.

places.name: La Cusquenita
places.note: Sunday adobo is the reason locals fill this place before noon.

places.name: Quinta Eulalia
places.note: Old-school picanteria doing adobo and other quinta staples at weekend lunch.

places.name: Mercado de San Pedro
places.note: Breakfast counters ladle out adobo and caldo de gallina from early morning.

food.name: Alpaca steak and anticuchos
food.desc: Lean alpaca grilled as a steak with Andean grains, or beef-heart anticucho skewers charred over coals with potato and aji.

places.name: Pachapapa
places.note: Clay-oven grill in a colonial courtyard; alpaca and anticuchos are the signatures.

places.name: Cicciolina
places.note: Long-running Triunfo Street favorite; tapas bar downstairs, alpaca dishes upstairs.

places.name: Morena Peruvian Kitchen
places.note: Modern take on Cusqueno recipes, popular with travelers wanting a lighter room.

food.name: Chicha morada and chicha de jora
food.desc: Chicha morada is a sweet purple-corn drink with pineapple and clove; chicha de jora is the lightly fermented maize beer of the Andes.

places.name: Mercado de San Pedro
places.note: Juice row pours fresh chicha morada by the glass or pitcher, very cheap.

places.name: La Cusquenita
places.note: Serves both chichas alongside the picanteria food, as locals drink them.

places.name: Chicherias of San Sebastian
places.note: Houses flying a red flag or balloon sell home-brewed chicha de jora; ask before entering.

food.name: Pisco sour
food.desc: Peru's national cocktail: pisco, lime, sugar syrup, egg white and Angostura bitters, shaken to a foam. Coca tea is the local altitude alternative.

places.name: Museo del Pisco
places.note: Pisco bar and tasting room with flights, live music and knowledgeable bartenders.

places.name: Limbus Resto Bar
places.note: Hillside terrace with the best cocktail view over the city; book ahead at sunset.

places.name: Chicha por Gaston Acurio
places.note: Acurio's Cusco restaurant with a well-run bar and regional pisco infusions.

landmarks: Plaza de Armas
The magnificent colonial heart of the Inca capital, ringed by carved wooden balconies, twin churches and mountains, buzzing from morning processions to nightfall.
Sacsayhuamán
Zigzag ramparts of hundred-tonne stones fitted with astonishing precision crown the hill above Cusco, the greatest surviving monument of Inca military architecture.
Qorikancha (Temple of the Sun)
The empire's holiest temple, once sheathed in gold, survives as flawless Inca masonry beneath the colonial church of Santo Domingo.
Cusco Cathedral
A century in the building, this Renaissance-Baroque colossus on the plaza brims with Cusqueña School paintings, including the famous guinea-pig Last Supper.
Barrio de San Blas
Cusco's artisan quarter climbs steep whitewashed lanes to a tiny plaza, packed with galleries, cafés and the church's legendary carved pulpit.
Hatun Rumiyoc and the Twelve-Angled Stone
Along an Inca palace wall, one perfectly fitted twelve-cornered block has become the emblem of Cusco's mind-bending stonework.
Mercado Central de San Pedro
A riot of fruit-juice ladies, cheese wheels, chocolate, flowers and steaming soup stalls, Cusco's central market is pure sensory Peru.
Q'enqo
A carved limestone outcrop above the city concealing zigzag libation channels and a subterranean altar used in Inca rituals of sacrifice and astronomy.
Tambomachay
Known as the Inca's Bath, spring water still flows through elegant stone fountains at this ceremonial site honouring water just outside Cusco.
Cristo Blanco
An eight-metre white Christ gifted by Palestinian refugees stands beside Sacsayhuamán, arms outstretched over the best free panorama of Cusco's rooftops.

train.note: Machu Picchu trains mostly no longer start in central Cusco: both PeruRail and Inca Rail sell a bimodal bus-plus-train product from Cusco, and since 1 September 2025 PeruRail has used Pachar as the transfer point on selected departures rather than Ollantaytambo. Many travellers skip the packaged bus and take a colectivo straight to Ollantaytambo station, which has the fullest timetable; Poroy on the city's edge is no longer in regular use and San Pedro in Cusco itself serves mainly the Hidroelectrica local run. PeruRail also works the southern line to Puno with the daytime Titicaca train and the Belmond Andean Explorer sleeper, which continues to Arequipa. Peru runs no international passenger trains, so nothing crosses from Cusco to Bolivia, Chile or Brazil by rail, and Machu Picchu tickets should be booked well ahead in the June to August peak because train seats and entry slots sell out together.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches use the Terminal Terrestre de Cusco in the Santiago district, about 15 minutes by taxi from the Plaza de Armas, and a small terminal fee is payable before boarding. Cruz del Sur (https://www.cruzdelsur.com.pe/), Oltursa (https://www.oltursa.pe/), Civa and Turismo Mer cover the domestic network to Lima in around 21 hours, Arequipa in about 10, Puno in roughly 7 and Abancay in 5. Bolivia Hop and its sister Peru Hop run hop-on hop-off coaches through to Copacabana and La Paz, crossing at Kasani or Desaguadero with staff on board to walk passengers through the exit and entry stamps, which is the main reason travellers pay a premium over local buses. Local carriers also sell Cusco to La Paz through-tickets at the terminal, usually 12 hours or more with a change in Puno; most nationalities get a Bolivian stamp on arrival, but US citizens should check visa requirements first.

ferry.note: Cusco is a landlocked Andean city at about 3,400 m with no navigable water of its own, and the nearest passenger boats are the Lake Titicaca launches to the Uros, Taquile and Amantani islands, which leave from Puno some seven hours away by road.

half.name: Pisac
half.blurb: Sacred Valley town with steep Inca agricultural terraces above a hillside ruin and a lively daily crafts market.

half.name: Ollantaytambo
half.blurb: Living Inca town with a massive terraced fortress and original stone streets still laid out on their ancient grid.

half.name: Maras and Moray
half.blurb: Concentric Inca agricultural terraces shaped like an amphitheater near hillsides of centuries-old salt pans still worked by hand.

full.name: Rainbow Mountain (Vinicunca)
full.blurb: Multicolored mineral-streaked peak reached by a high-altitude drive and hike, one of the most photographed landscapes near Cusco.

full.name: Humantay Lake
full.blurb: Turquoise glacial lake beneath a snow-capped peak, reached by a steep high-altitude hike from the village of Soraypampa.

full.name: Machu Picchu
full.blurb: Fifteenth-century Inca citadel perched on a mountain ridge, reached by train through the Sacred Valley to Aguas Calientes.
